analysis.one_liner: Cuts estate tax rates by 20 percent and shields the first $3 million of an estate from tax.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan pair of House members proposed cutting estate tax rates 20% and exempting the first $3 million of an estate, but the bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut every federal estate tax rate by 20% and raise the amount of an estate shielded from tax to $3 million, with that threshold rising with inflation in later years. The tax applies when someone dies and passes property to heirs; the credit change would also cover gifts made during life. Only the largest estates pay estate tax at all, so the benefits would go overwhelmingly to the wealthiest families, while the lost revenue would have to be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of estates worth more than $3 million, who would pay 20% less tax on everything above that amount. Wealthy individuals making large lifetime gifts would also gain, since the same credit shields gifts from tax.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts every estate tax rate by 20% — for example, the top rate on estates above $2 million would drop from 49% to 39.2%.
Raises the unified credit so the first $3 million of an estate is exempt from estate and gift tax.
Increases the $3 million exemption each year after 2003 to keep pace with the cost of living, rounded to the nearest $10,000.
Applies to deaths and gifts occurring after enactment, so the relief would take effect immediately.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers generally, since the estate tax is one of the most concentrated taxes in the code — cutting it means less revenue that must be replaced by other taxes, higher deficits, or less spending.

drawbacks.text: The bill cuts rates on estates as small as $10,000 at the bottom of the schedule, but because most estates owe little or nothing, the dollars saved concentrate in the largest fortunes above the $3 million exemption.
Raising the unified credit also exempts large lifetime gifts from gift tax, letting the wealthiest families move up to $3 million — more with inflation — to heirs tax-free before death.
Reducing estate tax collections shrinks federal revenue, which under general principles of the budget must be offset by other taxes or borrowing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is real but narrowly aimed. A $3 million exemption already protects all but the largest estates from the tax, so the extra 20% rate cut and higher threshold would mostly benefit families with multi-million-dollar fortunes. Meanwhile the lost revenue is a cost shared by everyone. Congress had already enacted a phase-down of the estate tax in 2001, so this bill would have deepened that tax cut for the wealthiest estates at additional cost to the Treasury.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2003 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never considered it, and it expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Nita Lowey introduced the bill on July 9, 2003, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax bills.
Five members cosponsored it — four Democrats and one Republican.
The committee took no further action on the bill, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept estate tax collections on the schedule then in law, and the wealthiest estates did not receive the additional 20% rate cut the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; the largest estates gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Nita Lowey
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Ways and Means Committee.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship mix was unusual — a Democrat sponsored the estate tax cut with four Democratic and one Republican cosponsors — but the bill never reached a vote, so no partisan breakdown exists.

industries.note: The bill would cut their estate and gift tax bills by 20% on everything above a $3 million exemption. Because very few ordinary families owe any estate tax, the tax relief flows to them while the revenue loss is spread across all taxpayers.
